ctx-new-orleans.prompt: The Treaty of Ghent had been signed, yet a battle was fought at New Orleans. Which observation explains this best?
options: The commanders knew the peace terms but ignored them.
The gap between the signing and the news arriving was long enough to decide when the war effectively ended.
The British army never recognized the treaty.
At the time nobody was thinking of making a treaty.
ctx-new-orleans.explain: According to the sources the signing was on 24 December 1814, but on 8 January neither the armies nor Congress knew about it; so the issue was not intent but the journey of the news. The first option is tempting because we are used to explaining wars by the will of decision-makers; here the decision had been made, it simply had not arrived. The other two options do not match the sources.

ctx-lens.prompt: A municipal decision is announced only by a paper pinned to a wall. One day the same decision is relayed by telegraph to three different cities the same evening. Which of the four answers changed most?
options: Who is able to speak (production cost)
How far and how fast it gets (reach and speed)
Whether the receiver can answer back
Which language the decision text is written in
ctx-lens.explain: The telegraph carries a message to distant cities the same evening; what changes most is reach and speed. Who can speak may look tempting because the telegraph was costly and few people could use it, but in the example the speaker is the same (the municipality); what changed is the distance. Feedback and language do not change at all in the scenario.

time-ladder.prompt: Put these five events in order, oldest first.
items: The printing of the Diamond Sutra
The one-cent Sun appears in New York
The first message on Morse’s telegraph line
The Lumière brothers’ first paid screening
time-ladder.explain: The order is: Diamond Sutra (868), The Sun (1833), the telegraph (1844), the Lumière screening (1895), KDKA (1920). The trap: thinking of printing as something that “starts with Gutenberg” and placing nothing before the 1450s; yet a dated printed book goes back to 868. And do not confuse the penny press with the telegraph: The Sun came out about ten years before the telegraph.

claim-core.prompt: True or false: The invention of a communication technology alone determines what its social outcome will be.
claim-core.explain: False. Movable type was invented in China but did not become dominant there; in Europe the same idea, in a different economic and political environment, gave very different results. What makes “true” tempting is seeing the change that follows an invention and looking for the cause only in the machine.

concepts-glossary.prompt: Match each term with its correct definition.
pairs: A note naming the printer, place and date
An organization that gathers news once and sells it to many newspapers
concepts-glossary.explain: A colophon is a book’s “credits”; the fact that the 42-line Bible lacks one is among the reasons that tying the book to Gutenberg is hard. A firman is the sultan’s order and a fatwa is the chief mufti’s opinion; mixing the two up is a common exam error because in Müteferrika’s permission the two stand side by side. A news agency produces not the newspaper but the news sold to newspapers.

concepts-broadcast.text: The word “broadcast” was first used for {{1}}; its use for radio is recorded around the {{2}}.

options: scattering seed over a field
distributing letters
casting a fishing net

concepts-broadcast.explain: According to etymological records the word is agricultural in origin (seed scattered over a wide area) and the radio sense appears around 1921–22. “Distributing letters” may sound tempting because broadcasting has a counterpart in the paper world too; but the word’s origin is not about letters, it is about sowing. The 1820s option confuses the radio era with the age of the telegraph and the newspaper.

assump-gutenberg.prompt: Which of the following statements is consistent with the lesson’s sources?
options: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type is in Europe.
The oldest dated printed book is the Chinese Diamond Sutra of 868; in Korea a book was also printed with metal type in 1377.
The colophon of the Gutenberg Bible names the press and the date.
Movable type did not spread in China because it was never tried there.
assump-gutenberg.explain: The Diamond Sutra is 868, the Jikji 1377; both are older than the Gutenberg Bible. The first option is the most common myth; the Jikji was printed with metal type 78 years before the Bible. The third is wrong because the 42-line Bible has neither a title page nor a colophon. The fourth is wrong too: movable type was tried in China in the 1040s, and it did not spread there not because it was untried but because block printing stayed cheaper.

hiw-gutenberg-docs.prompt: Which is the most important contemporary document we have today about Gutenberg’s printing venture?
options: The colophon at the end of the 42-line Bible giving his name and the year
The Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of 1455 summarizing the hearing between him and Fust
A letter from Martin Luther to Gutenberg
A workshop ledger kept in Gutenberg’s own hand
hiw-gutenberg-docs.explain: According to the sources the main contemporary document is the notarial instrument of 6 November 1455. The colophon option is tempting because we assume “the famous book must have its credits”; but the 42-line Bible has neither a title page nor a colophon. For the other two options there is no basis in the sources.

hiw-newspaper.prompt: According to Weber, which of the following was not among the elements in place around 1600 for the birth of the newspaper?
options: The technique of book printing
A regular postal line open to the public
A network of professional correspondents
Telegraph lines
hiw-newspaper.explain: Weber says the newspaper became possible through printing technique, a regular postal relay and a network of correspondents; the telegraph comes two centuries later (1844). The last option is tempting because news and the telegraph are linked in our minds; but the speed of news in 1605 was the speed of the horse and the post.

hiw-penny.prompt: A new newspaper owner, reasoning that “the more readers, the more advertising income”, decides to sell his paper very cheaply, one copy at a time on the street. Whose logic does this choice resemble in history?
options: The state-issued official gazette (like Takvim-i Vekayi)
A newsletter copied by hand and sold to wealthy subscribers
The penny press
Radio broadcasting
hiw-penny.explain: Street sales one copy at a time, a low price and advertising income are the business model of the penny press that began with The Sun in 1833. The official gazette was issued for the state and the handwritten newsletter for wealthy subscribers; neither was built on selling to the crowd in the street. Radio broadcasting is another channel and another period.

hiw-wire.prompt: True or false: The transatlantic telegraph cable laid in 1858 worked without interruption until the new cable of 1866.
hiw-wire.explain: False. The 1858 cable worked on 5 August and became unusable on 18 September, so it lasted about six weeks; the permanent link was made on 27 July 1866. “True” is tempting because a historical “first” is often assumed to be lasting; yet a failed first attempt is normal in the history of technology.

hiw-image.prompt: A historian says, “photography was invented in 1839, so newspapers printed photographs from 1839 on.” What is the biggest problem with this inference?
options: Photography was invented not in 1839 but in 1939.
Taking a photograph and printing it in a newspaper were not the same technical problem; the halftone technique entered the newspaper only in 1880.
Newspapers deliberately refused to print photographs.
Photography spread only in Germany.
hiw-image.explain: Between the invention of photography and its printing in a newspaper there are some forty years: the first halftone photograph entered a newspaper in 1880, and its adaptation to rotary presses came in 1897. The first option is historically wrong; the third and fourth have no counterpart in the sources. The real lesson: an invention becomes a social event only when it connects to the technique another medium needs.

hiw-broadcast.prompt: Why is the BBC’s 1936 television service called “the world’s first regular high-definition television service” rather than simply “the first television service”?
options: Because the BBC broadcast only during the day.
Because Germany had started a regular but 180-line, low-definition service a year earlier; “first” depends on the criterion.
Because the BBC broadcast television in colour.
Because television had actually been invented in 1920, not 1936.
hiw-broadcast.explain: According to the sources Germany began a regular but 180-line service in 1935; the BBC’s 405 lines meet the high-definition criterion. So the word “first” is right only with a qualifier such as “high-definition”. The colour option may tempt; but colour broadcasting on the BBC began in 1967 on BBC Two, not at the 1936 opening.

evid-print.prompt: A researcher sees that cities with printing presses grew faster. What would your most basic objection be?
options: The press never reached the cities.
Printers may simply have chosen rich, crowded cities; so the cause of growth may be the cities’ earlier condition, not the press.
Growth can only be measured after 1600.
Protestantism spread the press, the press did not spread Protestantism; so the findings are meaningless.
evid-print.explain: The objection is the selection problem (which cities got presses); Dittmar’s study addresses exactly this: cities with presses had no earlier advantage, and distance from Mainz was used as a tool. The last option is tempting because the direction problem is a genuine worry; but we read that Rubin also tackles it with the same tool, so calling the findings “meaningless” goes too far.

evid-broadcast.prompt: What is the mechanism Gentzkow proposes for television lowering voter turnout?
options: Television broadcasts openly urged voters not to go to the polls.
People moved away from the newspapers and radio that carry more politics and turned to television; political knowledge fell.
The incomes of households that owned televisions fell.
In its first years television only broadcast election programmes.
evid-broadcast.explain: The author shows that television’s arrival coincided with sharp drops in newspaper and radio consumption and in political knowledge; that the effect was greatest in off-year congressional elections, which newspapers cover a lot and television little, supports the mechanism. The “open urging” option is tempting because “the media influenced me” makes us think first of propaganda; here the effect comes through a shift of attention.

crit-fear.prompt: How did the 16th–17th-century scholars whom Ann Blair studied respond to the worry of “too many books”?
options: They banned book printing.
They stopped reading books and went back to oral tradition.
They developed tools such as the alphabetical index, reference books and note-taking shortcuts.
They ignored the worry completely.
crit-fear.explain: Blair shows that scholars answered the abundance with indexes, reference works and selective reading and note-taking strategies. The banning option is tempting because we think “the first reaction to new technology is a ban”; here the reaction was to produce new tools.

crit-pyramid.prompt: A student writes, “the inverted pyramid was born of the telegraph’s unreliability and became standard during the Civil War.” According to Pöttker’s finding, which is the strongest counter-argument?
options: The telegraph was never used in newspapers.
A content analysis of two major newspapers shows the inverted pyramid became widespread only about twenty years later, in the 1880s.
No news was written during the Civil War.
The inverted pyramid was born only in Europe.
crit-pyramid.explain: Pöttker’s content analysis shows the inverted pyramid spread not during the Civil War but two decades later; that weakens the telegraph–Civil War explanation historically. “The telegraph was not used” may tempt because ignoring the tool seems an easy way to refute a technology explanation; but the refutation comes not from the tool’s absence but from the date of the phenomenon.

today-digital.prompt: A student says, “when the internet came, newspapers and television died.” What does Pew Research’s 2025 data say about this claim?
options: It confirms the claim: nobody gets news from television or print any more.
It weakens the claim: 64 per cent of US adults at least sometimes get news from television and 25 per cent from print publications.
It weakens the claim: social media is the only platform people get news from.
The data say nothing about news habits.
today-digital.explain: According to Pew’s August 2025 survey digital devices are the most common (86 per cent), but television (64 per cent), radio (44 per cent) and print (25 per cent) are still used. The third option contradicts the fact that social media is at 53 per cent and is not the only platform. Note: this data covers only US adults and “at least sometimes” use; it says nothing about Turkey.

today-lab.prompt: A student reads a news agency text in the morning, listens to a radio bulletin in the afternoon, watches a series in the evening and writes a comment under a video at night. Which main observation of the lesson does this day illustrate?
options: New media completely remove the old.
Media born in different periods are used together in the same day, layer upon layer.
Only social media is a source of news.
Radio and television are widespread only in Turkey.
today-lab.explain: In one day a news agency text from the 1835 tradition, the radio of the 1920s, television-style broadcasting and the network are used together; that is layering. The first option is the commonest misconception in media history; even the Pew data show the old media persisting. The other two options do not fit the scenario or the sources.

turkey-ban.prompt: A student writes, “because the Ottomans banned printing, there was no press at all until 1727.” According to Schwartz’s article, which is the strongest counter-argument?
options: There was no press in the Ottoman lands before 1727 either; but there was no ban.
The ban was first written down in 1584 in a book printed in Paris, without a source; nobody claims to have seen the firmans; and a Jewish press had been working in Istanbul since 1493.
The ban firmans were found in Topkapı Palace but never published.
The press came to Istanbul not with Müteferrika but directly with Gutenberg.
turkey-ban.explain: Schwartz traces the ban claim to Thevet, shows that nobody claims to have seen the firmans, and that Jewish and Christian presses worked in the empire. The first option is half right (the Muslim-run press was set up in 1727) but “there was no press at all” is wrong; the question also asks for the argument’s source and grounds. The third option is invented: the article says the firmans have not been seen.

turkey-muteferrika.prompt: Which is correct about the scope of Müteferrika’s printing permission?
options: Only religious books were allowed to be printed.
Non-religious books such as dictionaries, history, medicine, astronomy and geography could be printed; jurisprudence, exegesis, hadith and theology were left out.
Every kind of book, the Quran included, could be printed freely.
Only translations from foreign languages could be printed.
turkey-muteferrika.explain: According to the firman as reported by Schwartz the restriction matches Müteferrika’s own wish in his treatise: non-religious fields. The first option is the opposite error; the commonest confusion is to think “printing was against religion” and to link the permission to religious books. The last is also wrong: although the first book was the Turkish translation of an Arabic dictionary, the permission was not limited to translation.

turkey-press.prompt: What is the most important feature that distinguishes Tercüman-ı Ahval from Takvim-i Vekayi?
options: Takvim-i Vekayi was not in Turkish, Tercüman-ı Ahval was.
Tercüman-ı Ahval was a private newspaper issued without state support; Takvim-i Vekayi was the state’s official gazette.
Tercüman-ı Ahval was the Ottoman Empire’s first newspaper.
Tercüman-ı Ahval was founded by a foreigner.
turkey-press.explain: The difference is ownership and source: Takvim-i Vekayi was the state gazette (1831); Tercüman-ı Ahval was issued by private enterprise without state support (1860). The first option is wrong because Takvim-i Vekayi had started with a Turkish original edition; and those who count Ceride-i Havadis as the “first private paper” overlook its English owner.

turkey-airwaves.text: The first radio broadcast in Turkey was made in {{1}} from Istanbul; the first test television broadcast was made in {{2}} from Ankara.
turkey-airwaves.explain: Istanbul Radio began broadcasting on 6 May 1927; the first television test broadcast was made on 31 January 1968 from the Mithatpaşa studio in Ankara. The other years match no event; the pair most often confused is TRT’s founding (1964) and the television test broadcast (1968): they are separate events.

exam-patterns.prompt: Exam question: “Which of the following is the first private newspaper in Turkish press history issued by Turks without state support?”
options: Takvim-i Vekayi
Ceride-i Havadis
Tercüman-ı Ahval
Tasvir-i Efkâr
exam-patterns.explain: Tercüman-ı Ahval (22 October 1860) is described this way. Takvim-i Vekayi is the state’s gazette (1831). Ceride-i Havadis (1840) is private but belonged to the Englishman William Churchill and was published with state permission; it is the most tempting wrong answer. Tasvir-i Efkâr (1862) is the fourth Turkish-language newspaper and Şinasi’s second venture.

summary.prompt: True or false: According to this lesson’s main idea, the invention of a new communication technology alone determines its social outcome and old media disappear when a new one comes.
summary.explain: False: the lesson argues that a technology offers an environment but the outcome is decided by the users and institutions, and that old media often do not vanish, they pile up. What makes “true” tempting is the brevity of the “technology is destiny” story.

quiz.prompt: Which is the oldest surviving dated printed book?
options: Gutenberg’s 42-line Bible
The Diamond Sutra (868)
The Jikji (1377)
The first issue of Takvim-i Vekayi
quiz.explain: The Diamond Sutra is dated 11 May 868 and printed with woodblocks. Gutenberg’s Bible is the tempting answer because the “printing = Gutenberg” pattern is widespread; yet even the Jikji (1377) is 78 years older than the Bible, and the 42-line Bible carries no date.

quiz.prompt: True or false: At the end of the 42-line Bible there is a colophon giving the printer’s name and the date.
quiz.explain: False. Catalogues note that the book has neither a title page nor a colophon, and that the attribution to Gutenberg rests today on general acceptance. What makes “true” tempting is the expectation that a famous book must have its “credits”.

quiz.prompt: Match each event with its year.
pairs: The launch of The Sun (New York)
quiz.explain: 1605 (newspaper), 1833 (penny press), 1844 (telegraph), 1895 (cinema), 1920 (radio broadcasting). The pair most often confused is The Sun and the telegraph: the penny press appeared about ten years before the telegraph; so the “street sale” that the penny press produced is an order that predates the telegraph.

quiz.prompt: Put these six events in Turkey in order, oldest first.
items: The publication of Müteferrika’s first book, the Vankulu Dictionary
The founding of the Anadolu Agency
The first broadcast of Istanbul Radio
The first test broadcast of TRT television
quiz.explain: The order is: the Vankulu Dictionary (1729), Takvim-i Vekayi (1831), Tercüman-ı Ahval (1860), the Anadolu Agency (1920), Istanbul Radio (1927), the television test broadcast (1968). The commonest mistake is to place Müteferrika at 1727 (the year of permission) or after Takvim-i Vekayi; the first book came out in 1729, that is, before both.

quiz.text: According to Weber the first regular printed news sheet appeared in {{1}} in the year {{2}}.

options: Strasbourg
London
Venice

quiz.explain: Johann Carolus’s Relation appeared in Strasbourg in 1605. The London option is tempting because the Oxford Gazette, issued there in 1665, became a symbol of English journalism; but that comes a century later and it was an official gazette posted to subscribers, not one sold in the street.

quiz.scenario: (Hypothetical scenario.) In a presentation a student makes two sentences: (a) “The inverted pyramid was born of the telegraph’s unreliability during the Civil War.” (b) “The printing press made Europe Protestant, because cities with presses became more Protestant.”

parts.prompt: What is the strongest source against sentence (a)?
options: Morse’s first telegraph message in 1844
Pöttker’s content analysis of the New York Herald and the New York Times: the inverted pyramid became widespread about twenty years later, in the 1880s
Reuters’ London office in 1851
parts.explain: Pöttker shows that the inverted pyramid became widespread not in the Civil War but in the decades after. The other two options show that the telegraph existed; but they do not refute the telegraph story, because the question is not whether the tool existed but when the phenomenon became widespread.

parts.prompt: What is the most balanced assessment of sentence (b)?
options: Rubin’s finding proves that the press alone created Protestantism.

Rubin found cities with presses at least 29 points more likely to be Protestant and used distance from Mainz as a tool; this is a strong association, but saying “is associated with and may have contributed to” is safer than “created it alone”.
The finding shows there is no relationship between the press and Protestantism.
parts.explain: Rubin’s study reports a strong association; but one study does not license a single-cause verdict. The first option turns an association into a single cause; the third says the opposite of the finding.

quiz.takeaway: Technology stories are seductive; ask two questions: is the date right, and at what level is the evidence?

quiz.prompt: Which pairing is correct for Müteferrika’s press?
options: 1727: first book; 1729: permission
1727: permission; 1729: first book (the Vankulu Dictionary)
1831: permission; 1727: first book
1729: Takvim-i Vekayi; 1727: permission
quiz.explain: The sources give the permission as July 1727 and the first book as 1729. The first option reverses the two; in exams the “year of permission” and the “year of the first book” are often confused. The third and fourth options mix Takvim-i Vekayi (1831) up with Müteferrika.

quiz.prompt: True or false: The firmans by which the Ottoman sultans banned printing in 1485 and 1515 have survived.
quiz.explain: False. Schwartz writes that she has come across no one who claims to have seen these firmans; the ban claim comes from an account Thevet wrote in 1584 without giving a source. What makes “true” tempting is that the claim has been repeated for centuries: repetition does not replace a document.

quiz.prompt: On what date and with what basic aim was the Anadolu Agency founded?
options: 6 April 1920; to make the National Struggle known to domestic and foreign publics
23 April 1920; to print parliamentary minutes
1 May 1964; to unify radio broadcasts
28 October 1938; to open Ankara Radio
quiz.explain: The agency was founded in Ankara on 6 April 1920 by Yunus Nadi and Halide Edib to make the National Struggle known to domestic and foreign publics. The other dates belong to other institutions: 1964 TRT, 1938 Ankara Radio; 23 April is not the agency’s founding date.

quiz.prompt: What is the main finding of Strömberg’s study of radio in the 1930s?
options: US counties with many radio listeners received more New Deal relief funds, even holding poverty and unemployment constant.
Radio spread only in rich counties.
Radio lowered voter turnout.
Radio had no political consequences.
quiz.explain: Strömberg finds that counties with many radio listeners received more relief and explains this by a new mass medium changing who is informed. The third option is tempting because the “turnout fell” finding belongs to television (Gentzkow).

quiz.prompt: According to Pew Research’s 2025 survey, which of the following has the lowest share among the platforms from which US adults at least sometimes get news?
options: Television
Radio
Print publications
Social media
quiz.explain: The shares: television 64 per cent, radio 44 per cent, social media 53 per cent, print publications 25 per cent. Print publications are the lowest; but not zero, so the sentence “the newspaper died” does not fit this data.

quiz.prompt: According to Dittmar (2011), by how much did European cities that got a printing press in the 1400s grow faster between 1500 and 1600 than similar cities?
options: 6 per cent
60 per cent
160 per cent
There was no difference
quiz.explain: Dittmar finds 60 per cent faster growth; the cities had no advantage before the press. The 6 per cent and 160 per cent options are typical decimal or zero slips when memorizing numbers.
